title: Undertow and Postcards
premise: When Paloma Eriksen returns to the fading coastal town of Vesterhavn for her mother's funeral, a stranger named Ilse addresses the family by their old, erased surname — a name tied to a drowned fisherman and a settlement payout the town has spent forty years pretending was charity. Translating her late mother's letters, Paloma discovers that the 'accident' at sea was witnessed, silenced, and bought. As demolition of the old harbor quarter approaches — the last physical archive of what happened — she must find the surviving witness before the town's most powerful family buries the truth under concrete. In the end, justice arrives not through courts but through testimony: Paloma reads the witness's account aloud at the final town meeting, and the demolition is halted long enough for a memorial to be carved into the new seawall.
about_author: Rosalind Eastwick is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent a decade translating testimony in coastal fishing communities. She writes about the words people lose on purpose, and lives within earshot of a working harbor.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Returning to Vesterhavn for her mother's funeral, Paloma catalogs everything the family never discussed, including the old surname no one uses. The emotional beat is grief laced with suspicion: mourning a woman she loved but never fully understood.

chapters.title: A Stranger Says Our Name
chapters.summary: At the wake, an elderly woman named Ilse grips Paloma's wrist and says the family's pre-emigration name aloud. Paloma's brother Anders hustles the woman out. POV Paloma; the beat is vertigo — the ground of family identity tilting.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Paloma's POV, tracing how she lost her childhood language word by word through school, shame, and her mother's deliberate silence. Emotional beat: tender melancholy, establishing memory as something that can be stolen politely.

chapters.title: The Letters Under the Floor
chapters.summary: Sorting the house, Paloma finds loose floorboards and a tin of unsent letters in her mother's hand, half-written in the old tongue. POV Paloma. Beat: dread mixed with hunger — she can only partially read them, and knows someone else could.

chapters.title: Anders Wants the House Sold
chapters.summary: POV Anders. He pushes to sell quickly before the harbor-quarter demolition depresses prices, revealing he knew about the letters' existence years ago and chose silence. Beat: his guilt wearing pragmatism as a coat.

chapters.title: Ilse at the Breakwater
chapters.summary: Paloma tracks down Ilse, who begins telling the story of the night fisherman Joren Vale drowned in 1983 — and stops herself, saying some sentences are dangerous in this town. POV Paloma. Beat: the first true hook of the mystery.

chapters.title: The Halvorsen Name
chapters.summary: Paloma researches the town's founding families and finds the powerful Halvorsens received the harbor concession weeks after Joren's death, following a 'settlement.' POV Paloma. Beat: cold clarity as pattern replaces coincidence.

chapters.title: Mother's Half-Sentences
chapters.summary: Working through the letters, Paloma recognizes her mother's handwriting shifts — fear entering the script mid-1983. She translates fragments: 'I saw,' 'they offered,' 'the child must never.' POV Paloma. Beat: grief curdling into anger.

chapters.title: The Demolition Notice
chapters.summary: POV Ilse. She receives official notice that her cottage in the harbor quarter will be razed in six weeks — the building where she hid the night of the drowning. Beat: quiet terror; the past being scheduled for removal.

chapters.title: Dinner with the Halvorsens
chapters.summary: Town patriarch Edvard Halvorsen hosts a memorial reception and offers Paloma help 'with the estate,' probing gently about papers. His charm has teeth. POV Paloma. Beat: menace dressed as hospitality.

chapters.title: What Anders Buried
chapters.summary: Confrontation between siblings: Paloma accuses Anders of knowing; he admits their mother made him swear an oath at nineteen, trading silence for the family's safety. POV alternates. Beat: rupture — love and betrayal in the same room.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Signed Nothing
chapters.summary: Ilse reveals she was fourteen the night Joren drowned, saw the Halvorsen boat ram his skiff, and was coached by police to say nothing. Her signed statement exists but vanished from the file. POV Ilse. Beat: the weight of forty complicit years lifting slightly.

chapters.title: Archive Fire
chapters.summary: The municipal records room suffers a small, convenient fire; the 1983 maritime file is water-damaged beyond reading. POV Paloma. Beat: escalation — the enemy is active now, and time is burning too.

chapters.title: The Translator's Advantage
chapters.summary: Paloma realizes the letters' key passage is written in a dialect only she and one other living person share: Ilse. Together they decode it — her mother witnessed the collision from the cliff path and was paid to leave. POV both women. Beat: alliance forged in shared language.

chapters.title: Edvard Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Halvorsen offers Paloma a generous sum and a translated memorial plaque for her mother if the letters stay private. He mentions her career, her fragility, her brother's debts. POV Paloma. Beat: temptation rendered precisely, almost reasonable.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Machines
chapters.summary: Demolition moved up. Paloma, Ilse, and a reluctant Anders sneak into the condemned harbor quarter and recover a rusted box Ilse buried as a girl: Joren's logbook, salvaged from the wreck, naming the other vessel. POV Paloma. Beat: breathless, illicit hope.

chapters.title: Brother at the Door
chapters.summary: Halvorsen's men pressure Anders to hand over the logbook; instead he brings it to Paloma, finally choosing her side. POV Anders. Beat: redemption earned through a small, costly act.

chapters.title: Reading the Water
chapters.summary: Paloma translates the logbook's final entry publicly for the first time, and the town's older generation begins remembering aloud — small testimonies surfacing like bodies after a thaw. POV Paloma. Beat: rising crescendo, the town's silence cracking.

chapters.title: The Town Meeting
chapters.summary: Climax. At the meeting to approve final demolition, Paloma reads Ilse's full account and her mother's letter aloud, untranslated, then renders them into the town's language sentence by sentence. Halvorsen's son, learning his father's role, does not defend him. Beat: catharsis — speech as verdict.

chapters.title: What the Law Cannot Do
chapters.summary: No prosecution follows — statutes expired decades ago — but the concession is revoked, the demolition paused, and the seawall redesignated as a memorial site. POV Paloma. Beat: sober triumph; justice outside the law is still justice, but it costs.

chapters.title: Postcards to a Drowned Man
chapters.summary: Quiet epilogue-adjacent chapter: Paloma mails postcards to Joren Vale's last known address, writing in the recovered language, each one a piece of the story set down. POV Paloma. Beat: elegiac tenderness, language returning word by word.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: Final chapter. A year later, Paloma stays in Vesterhavn as the town's unofficial translator of its own records. Ilse teaches children the old tongue; the memorial stone bears both names, Vale and Eriksen. POV Paloma. Beat: resolution — memory kept is power returned.
